title: Rebekah at the well (Genesis 24)
hook: a servant prays for a sign, and a young woman waters ten camels

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sarah's grave, a field and a cave bought in grief, and your line was grief deserves ground. What loss did you give a place to? Day three hundred fifty-nine.

Genesis twenty-four is a road trip. Abraham is old now. Sarah is buried. Isaac is grown, and alone. So Abraham sends his oldest servant, the one who runs everything, back to the old country, to find a wife for Isaac among his own family. The servant loads up ten camels with gifts and sets out for Mesopotamia. He arrives at a well outside the city of Nahor at evening, the time when the women come out to draw water. And before he does anything else, he stops, and prays. Not for a beautiful bride. For something much more specific.
screen: `A ROAD TRIP FOR A WIFE.` → `TEN CAMELS, A LONG ROAD.` → `HE STOPS AT THE WELL AND PRAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the sign he asks for, in the King James Bible: let it be that the young woman I ask for a drink will say, "Drink, and I will give thy camels drink also." That's a very particular test. Anyone might give a stranger a sip of water. But a thirsty camel drinks a great deal, and he has ten of them. Offering to water them all means trip after trip down to the spring with a heavy jar, for a man she's never met. The servant isn't asking for a sign of luck. He's asking for a sign of character: generosity beyond what's asked. And then, the text says, before he had done speaking, Rebekah comes out with her jar on her shoulder. He asks for a little water. She says, drink, my lord, and lowers her jar. And then, unprompted: "I will draw water for thy camels also, until they have done drinking." She runs, again and again, until ten camels are done. The servant just watches, silent, amazed. In his prayer he asked God to show kindness to his master. The Hebrew word is chesed, loyal, generous love that goes beyond duty. It runs all through this chapter, and the servant sees it at the well. Then one more thing worth noticing. When the family asks whether she'll leave home and travel back with a stranger, they ask her directly. "Wilt thou go with this man? And she said, I will go." In Hebrew that answer is a single word, elekh, from the same verb God used when he told Abraham to go. The chapter ends far south, at evening, where Isaac has gone out into a field. He sees camels coming. He marries Rebekah, and he loves her, and he is comforted after his mother's death.
screen: `A VERY PARTICULAR SIGN.` · `TEN THIRSTY CAMELS.` · `CHESED: KINDNESS BEYOND DUTY.` · `WILT THOU GO? I WILL GO.` · then, large: `I WILL DRAW WATER FOR THY CAMELS ALSO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do more than you're asked. Settle, and breathe. Think of the small requests that will come your way in the next day. Can you grab me a glass of water? Can you send that file? Can you pick up milk? Pick one, and imagine Rebekah's answer: yes, and also. Fill their glass, and refill the pitcher. Send the file, and a note that saves them time. Not something huge. One more trip to the well. If you pray, you can ask for a generous heart. The bell holds the time.
Chesed. Hebrew for loyal, generous love that goes beyond duty: what the servant saw when Rebekah offered to water ten camels.
Your line: kindness to camels. Today, when someone asks a small favor, do it, and one thing more they didn't ask for. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Many Christians pray for guidance before big decisions, as Abraham's servant did, and the story of Rebekah is sometimes read at weddings and in teaching on generosity and hospitality.

original.note: Hebrew: loyal, generous love, kindness that goes beyond duty. It runs through Genesis 24.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sweet story about finding a wife.
what it means: a servant asks for a sign of character, and a young woman's generosity beyond what's asked answers his prayer.
what a scholar hears: chesed runs through the chapter; ten thirsty camels mean many trips to the spring; and Rebekah's I will go echoes Abraham's going.

notes: 'The longest chapter in the book' (Genesis 24, 67 verses). Confirm.
The servant is unnamed in Genesis 24; often identified with Eliezer (15:2). Script keeps him unnamed. Confirm.
Camel water intake: a very thirsty camel can drink over 100 liters (25+ gallons); stated as 'many gallons'. Confirm.
Distance from Canaan to Aram-naharaim/Nahor: several hundred miles; 'hundreds of miles'. Confirm.

Audit (10% sample): 'Two words, like Abraham's' was a miscount (English 'I will go' is three words; Hebrew elekh is one) and unclear; now says it is one Hebrew word from the same verb as God's 'go' to Abraham (Genesis 12:1, lekh lekha). Keeper: confirm elekh and the h-l-k link.
Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'the longest chapter in the book', 'hundreds of miles' (now 'Mesopotamia', 24:10) and 'many gallons'; hook screen heads updated to match.
